Laver
LAY-ver
n.
From Latin lavare, “to wash”; the bronze basin set between the tabernacle’s door and the brazen altar, at which the priests washed their hands and feet before entering the sanctuary or approaching the altar.

📖 Biblical Definition

The laver was the bronze basin set in the court of the tabernacle (later, in Solomon’s temple, a vastly larger bronze basin called the molten sea on twelve oxen, 1 Kgs 7:23-26) at which the priests washed their hands and feet before entering the sanctuary or approaching the altar to minister. Exodus 30:17-21 prescribes the laver: thou shalt also make a laver of brass, and his foot also of brass, to wash withal: and thou shalt put it between the tabernacle of the congregation and the altar, and thou shalt put water therein. For Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and their feet thereat: When they go into the tabernacle of the congregation, they shall wash with water, that they die not; or when they come near to the altar to minister, to burn offering made by fire unto the LORD: So they shall wash their hands and their feet, that they die not: and it shall be a statute for ever to them, even to him and to his seed throughout their generations. Several structural features mark the laver’s theological function. First, it stood between the altar and the sanctuary, geographically and ritually—the priest who had come past the altar of sacrifice now stood at the laver before proceeding further into the holy place. Atonement (the altar) preceded cleansing (the laver) preceded ministry (the sanctuary). Second, the failure to wash carried capital sanction: that they die not, repeated twice in the passage. The laver’s ritual was not optional but binding under death. Third, the laver was made from the looking-glasses of the women who served at the door of the tabernacle (Ex 38:8)—a detail of detailed significance: the mirrors by which the women had checked their outward appearance became the basin in which the priests examined themselves before approaching the LORD. Fourth, the laver had its New Covenant fulfillment in the cleansing the saint receives through the Word and the washing of regeneration. Ephesians 5:25-27: husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it; That he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word, That he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish. Titus 3:5: not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost. Hebrews 10:22: let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water. The laver therefore typifies the ongoing cleansing the saint receives at the throne of grace, by which he is fitted for the priestly service to which he has been called: regeneration washes him once; the Word and the Spirit continue to wash him daily; the discipline of self-examination at the laver fits him for the worship and service in which he approaches the LORD.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines LAVER as a vessel for washing; a bronze basin in the tabernacle and temple at which the priests washed before entering the sanctuary or approaching the altar; fulfilled in the New Covenant by the washing of regeneration and the daily cleansing by the Word.

expand to see more

LAVER, n. — 1. A vessel for washing; a basin. 2. A large brazen vessel placed in the outer court of the tabernacle, in which the priests washed their hands and feet, and the entrails of beasts that were to be offered as burnt sacrifices.

WASH, v.t. — To cleanse by means of water and rubbing; to remove dirt or filth by water. In scripture, to cleanse from sin by the blood of Christ, the washing of regeneration, and the cleansing of the Word.

📖 Key Scripture

Exodus 30:17-19 — "And the LORD spake unto Moses, saying, Thou shalt also make a laver of brass, and his foot also of brass, to wash withal: and thou shalt put it between the tabernacle of the congregation and the altar, and thou shalt put water therein. For Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and their feet thereat."

Exodus 38:8 — "And he made the laver of brass, and the foot of it of brass, of the lookingglasses of the women assembling, which assembled at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation."

Ephesians 5:25-27 — "Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it; That he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word, That he might present it to himself a glorious church..."

Titus 3:5 — "Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The laver-doctrine is corrupted, on one side, by the loss of the laver-typology in much contemporary preaching that has stopped tracing the Old Testament types to their New Testament fulfillments—and on the other by the sacramental over-reading that has identified the laver’s typological fulfillment exclusively with baptismal regeneration, against the broader NT teaching of the Word and the Spirit’s ongoing cleansing through Word and prayer.

expand to see more

The loss of the laver-typology is a wider symptom of the general loss of typological reading in much contemporary preaching. The Old Testament types—the tabernacle furnishings, the priestly garments, the sacrifices, the feasts, the persons of the patriarchs and judges—are no longer regularly traced to their New Testament fulfillments. The result is a Bible whose Old Testament is preached in isolation from its Christological substance and whose New Testament loses much of the depth the Old Testament types supply. The laver is one specific case: a basin between altar and sanctuary, prescribed under penalty of death, whose New Covenant fulfillment is the cleansing by the Word and the washing of regeneration that fits the saint for priestly service. To preach the laver as ancient cultic detail without tracing its typological substance is to miss what the Spirit who inspired both testaments was doing in the structure He gave.

The opposite corruption is the sacramental over-reading that has identified the laver’s typological fulfillment exclusively with baptismal regeneration—treating water-baptism as the once-for-all answer to the laver, with no acknowledgment of the ongoing cleansing by the Word the New Testament also teaches. Eph 5:26 specifies that Christ sanctifies and cleanses the church with the washing of water by the word: the Word itself is the cleansing means, applied across the believer’s lifetime. The laver-typology therefore points not only to the once-for-all regenerating washing at conversion but also to the ongoing cleansing by which the saint, daily approaching the throne of grace, is fitted for the worship and service in which he stands. Recover both ends. Refuse the loss of typology that abandons the laver-doctrine altogether, and refuse the sacramental over-reading that confines its fulfillment to baptism alone. The biblical laver typifies both the regenerating washing at conversion (Tit 3:5) and the ongoing Word-and-Spirit cleansing across the Christian life (Eph 5:26), by which the priestly saint is daily fitted for the holy service to which he has been called.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin lavare (to wash); the bronze basin between the tabernacle’s altar and sanctuary, at which the priests washed before service (Ex 30:17-21); typologically fulfilled in the washing of regeneration (Tit 3:5) and the ongoing cleansing by the Word (Eph 5:26).

expand to see more

Hebrew kiyyōr (H3595) — basin, laver (the OT word; Ex 30:18; 1 Kgs 7:30, 38).

Hebrew yām (H3220) — sea (the “molten sea” in Solomon’s temple, 1 Kgs 7:23-26; the great bronze laver on twelve oxen).

Greek loutron (G3067) — a washing, laver (Eph 5:26; Tit 3:5).

Greek louō (G3068) — to wash, bathe (Heb 10:22).
